body.x: Families read hundreds of profiles, and most blur together within a minute: a list of adjectives, a line about being "family-oriented", nothing a parent can repeat at the dinner table. Your bio has one job — to give the right family enough true, specific material to start a conversation, and to let the wrong family pass by without wasting anyone's time. Below is a blueprint for Shia seekers, two complete example bios built on it, and the phrases that quietly sink good profiles.
The opener: two honest sentences about a real life

Open with who you are and where your life actually happens — not a slogan. "Assalamu alaikum, I am Ahmed, 29, a civil engineer living in Birmingham, where I was born and where my parents still live" does more work than any adjective, because a reader can immediately picture the life being proposed. Add one human detail that is true and checkable: coaching the under-12s at football, running your grandfather's bookshop on weekends, learning to cook your mother's biryani properly. One concrete detail gives a family something to ask about; five adjectives give them nothing.
Faith and practice, written as habits rather than labels

This is the section seekers most often get wrong, writing either nothing or a scorecard. Families do not need a label like "very religious" — they need to recognise a daily life. Describe practice as habits: "I pray five times a day, attend Thursday night duas at our local centre when work allows, and fast through Ramadan." For the marja line, plain and unapologetic is the tasteful way: "I follow Ayatullah Sistani" — one factual line, stated the way you would state your city. If you are growing in practice, say so honestly: "I am working on consistency in my prayers" beats a perfection no one believes.
Education and work: the facts a family will verify anyway

State your qualification, your field, and where you are based, in one or two lines. "BSc in computer science, working as a data analyst in Manchester for three years; hoping to stay in the North West" answers the three questions every family asks first. If your path is less conventional — a trade, your own business, a career change — describe it plainly. A skilled electrician who writes clearly about his work reads as a stronger prospect than a vague "businessman" with no detail. Avoid salary figures and promises stated as facts; stability and honesty show in how you write.
Family and the life around you

Two or three sentences: parents, siblings, where you fit, and what family life looks like in practice. "I am the eldest of three; my father runs a small grocery business and my mother teaches at a weekend madrasa. We live close to my grandparents and most Fridays are spent at their house." This tells a prospective spouse what they are joining. If your situation needs a sentence of context — parents divorced, a parent passed away, a non-Muslim family of your own — give it that one honest sentence here. Discovered late, these things feel hidden; stated early, they are simply your life.
What you are looking for — including deal-breakers, stated kindly

Describe the person, not a shopping list. Lead with character and direction: "I am looking for a spouse who values her deen, enjoys family life, and wants a home where the Quran is read and guests are welcome." Then the practical shape: age range, whether you would consider someone from another city or country, whether you are open to a spouse who is divorced or widowed. Deal-breakers belong here too, firm without being harsh — framed as your situation, not a judgement on others. "I plan to remain in Birmingham near my parents, so I am looking for someone happy to settle here" is firm and kind. "No one from back home" is the same fact written as an insult.
Two bios written to this blueprint

For a son: "Assalamu alaikum. I am Bilal, 28, a pharmacist living and working in Leicester. I was born in the UK; my parents came from Karachi and live ten minutes away, and I am the second of four siblings. I pray five times a day and follow Ayatullah Sistani; our family attends the local Shia centre, where I volunteer with the youth group during Muharram. Outside work I play five-a-side and am teaching myself Urdu so I can speak to my grandmother properly. I am looking for a spouse who is serious about her deen and her own growth, who enjoys a busy family home, and who would be happy to build our life in the Midlands."

For a daughter: "Assalamu alaikum. I am Maryam, 25, a primary school teacher from Lucknow, living with my parents and younger brother. I completed my BEd two years ago and teach at a school near our home. I wear hijab, pray regularly, and our family follows Ayatullah Sistani; Thursday evenings and the nights of Muharram are spent at the imambargah with my mother and aunts. I enjoy cooking and help run a weekend Quran class for young girls in our mohalla. I am looking for a husband who is practising, kind to his parents, and settled in his work, and who values a simple, family-centred life. I would prefer to settle in India. My father manages this profile with me."
Phrases that quietly kill a profile

"No time-wasters" — it only sounds like a warning about you
"Bio will be updated later" — families pass within seconds
"Looking for a religious but modern girl" — two labels that mean different things to every reader
"My family is very well known" — unverifiable, and sounds like the profile's only asset
"DM for pics" — signals exactly the approach serious families are avoiding
"Only serious people should contact" — a demand where an invitation should be
"I don't like writing about myself" — then no one can write you into their family's future either

Before you save, read your bio as a parent on the other side would: could they describe your child to their spouse in two sentences? Could they name one thing to ask about, one fact about your practice, and one clear sense of the life on offer? If yes, the bio is doing its job. Update it when your life changes — a finished course, a new job, a settled decision about location — because a current bio tells families this search is active and cared for.

title: What to put in your matrimony profile bio
